unit.title: Communicate information relating to work activities

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

From what she can remember of the week

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe how a supervisor should gather, check and organise information for a weekly report on her team's work.
essays.modelAnswer: She should first be clear what the report is for and what the manager needs, such as output against target, quality problems, staffing and issues needing a decision. She then gathers information from reliable sources: system reports, job sheets, timesheets, quality logs and the handover book, and asks team leaders for short notes on problems and causes. She records where each figure came from. Before using the figures, she checks them: totals are added again, figures are compared with the source records, and any figure that looks unusual, such as a sudden jump in errors, is queried. She also checks that nothing is missing, for example a day with no data. Opinions are kept separate from facts. She then organises the report under clear headings, such as summary, results against targets, issues and actions needed, with the most important points first. Figures go into a simple table or chart, and the summary at the top states the two or three things the manager most needs to know. She keeps the source records so that any figure can be explained if asked.
markingPoints: Clarifies the purpose and what the manager needs
Gathers from reliable sources and records where figures came from
Checks figures against sources, re-adds totals and queries unusual or missing data
Separates fact from opinion
Organises under headings with main points first, tables or charts and a summary; keeps sources

essays.stem: Explain how to give clear work instructions to a team for a new procedure, and how to check that they have understood.
essays.modelAnswer: The supervisor should first make sure she understands the new procedure fully and has the written version ready. She should choose a time when the team can listen without being rushed, and a place without much noise. She should begin by explaining why the change is being made, as people follow instructions better when they see the reason. She then goes through the steps in order, using short sentences and plain words, explaining any new terms, and showing each step where possible, for example on screen or with the actual forms. Each person should get a copy of the written steps, numbered and clearly laid out, in a format they can use. She should invite questions throughout. To check understanding, she should not simply ask whether everyone understands, since people may say yes to avoid embarrassment. Instead, she can ask open questions, such as 'What do you do if the customer has no receipt?', ask a team member to explain the steps back, and have each person carry out the procedure once while she watches. She should follow up after a few days to check it is being done correctly.
markingPoints: Prepares: understands the procedure, has written steps, suitable time and place
Explains the reason for the change
Gives steps in order in plain language, demonstrates, provides numbered written copy
Checks understanding with open questions, explain-back and a practical try
Follows up later to confirm correct practice

essays.stem: Compare face-to-face briefings, email, team messaging apps and notice boards for passing work information to a team. Recommend which to use for three different kinds of message.
essays.modelAnswer: Face-to-face briefings allow questions, show tone and body language, and suit important or sensitive news, but they take time and people who are absent miss them. Email gives a written record, can carry attachments and reaches everyone, but it is easily ignored when inboxes are full, and tone can be misread. Team messaging apps are fast and suit short, urgent updates, but messages scroll away, they can intrude on personal time, and private data must not be shared on them. Notice boards, physical or online, suit standing information that people need to look up, such as rotas, safety notices and procedures, but they are passive and people may not check them. For a change to a work procedure, I would use a face-to-face briefing followed by an email with the written steps, so people can ask questions and also keep a record. For urgent news, such as a site closure or a system failure, a team messaging app or group alert is best because it is immediate, with confirmation that each person has seen it. For the monthly duty rota, a notice board or shared online folder is best, with a short message to say it has been posted.
markingPoints: Face-to-face: questions and tone; time and absence limits
Email: record and reach; overload and tone limits
Messaging apps: speed; intrusion, scrolling and data limits
Notice boards: standing information; passive
Recommends a suitable channel for three different message types, with reasons

essays.stem: Plan a shift handover system for a team that works around the clock, such as a security company or a call centre.
essays.modelAnswer: The system needs a set time, a set method and a set record. I would schedule a ten-minute overlap between shifts, so the outgoing and incoming supervisors can speak face to face, and the incoming team can be briefed before they start. A standard handover log, kept on paper or in a shared system, would have fixed headings: incidents and complaints during the shift, work still open and who owns it, urgent matters for the next shift, equipment faults, visitors or deliveries expected, and staffing changes. The outgoing supervisor completes it before the overlap, so nothing is forgotten in the rush. During the overlap, the supervisors go through the log together, the incoming supervisor asks questions, and both sign and time it. The incoming supervisor then gives a short briefing to the team. Urgent safety or security matters are handed over in person, never by log alone. Logs are kept for the period set by policy so they can be checked later. Each month, the manager samples logs and asks staff whether anything has been missed, and the format is improved where needed.
markingPoints: Set overlap time for face-to-face handover
Standard log with fixed headings (incidents, open work, urgent items, faults, expected events, staffing)
Log completed before the overlap, discussed, signed and timed by both supervisors
Urgent safety matters handed over in person; team briefed by incoming supervisor
Logs kept and reviewed; system improved over time

essays.stem: Describe what an incident report should contain and how it should be written, and explain why facts must be kept separate from opinions.
essays.modelAnswer: An incident report should give the date, time and exact place of the incident; the names and roles of the people involved and of any witnesses; a clear, step-by-step description of what happened; any injury or damage and the first aid or other action taken; the conditions at the time, such as lighting or a wet floor; and who was informed and when. It should end with any immediate steps taken to make the area safe, and suggestions to prevent a repeat, clearly marked as suggestions. The report should be written as soon as possible, while memories are fresh, in plain language and the past tense. Measurements, times and quotes from witnesses should be exact. It should be signed and dated by the writer. Facts must be kept separate from opinions because the report may be used to find the cause, to decide on improvements, for insurance claims and sometimes in legal or disciplinary matters. If the writer guesses or blames, for example by calling someone careless, the report becomes unfair and unreliable, and the real cause may be missed. Opinions, if needed, should be clearly labelled.
markingPoints: Contents: date, time, place, people and witnesses, what happened
Contents: injury or damage, action taken, conditions, who was informed, preventive suggestions
Written promptly, in plain language, with exact details, signed and dated
Explains uses of the report (cause, prevention, insurance, legal or disciplinary)
Explains why facts must be separate from opinion (fairness, reliability, real cause)

essays.stem: Evaluate how a supervisor should handle confidential and personal information at work.
essays.modelAnswer: A supervisor handles much sensitive information: staff addresses, pay, health and leave records, appraisal and disciplinary notes, and customers' details. Mishandling it can hurt people, break trust, damage the firm's name and break the data protection law. The first principle is need to know: information is shared only with those who need it for their work, not with curious colleagues. Personal data should be collected only for a clear purpose and used only for that purpose. Records must be stored securely: paper files in locked cabinets, electronic files in folders with restricted access and strong passwords, and screens locked when unattended. Confidential matters should be discussed in private, not in corridors or open offices, and should not be sent through personal email or chat groups. Information should be kept accurate and up to date, and disposed of safely by shredding or secure deletion when the retention period ends. The supervisor should also guide her team, since most breaches happen by mistake. These steps take some effort, but they are far less costly than the harm done by a leak, so they are well worth it.
markingPoints: Identifies types of sensitive information and the harm from mishandling
Need-to-know principle and use only for the stated purpose
Secure storage (locked files, restricted folders, passwords, locked screens) and private discussion
No personal email or chat groups; accuracy and safe disposal
Guides the team and weighs effort against harm

essays.stem: Explain how to present figures in a work report, using tables, charts, averages and percentages, so that a manager can act on them.
essays.modelAnswer: Figures help a manager only if their meaning is clear at a glance. Tables suit exact figures that the reader may want to look up, such as output for each shift on each day; they should have a title, clear row and column headings, units and totals. Charts suit trends and comparisons: a line chart for change over months, a column chart to compare teams, and a pie chart only for parts of a whole with few slices. Each chart needs a title, labelled axes and a scale that starts at zero unless there is a good reason. Averages summarise a set of figures, for example daily orders over a week, but the report should note any unusual day that pulls the average up or down. Percentages make different-sized figures comparable, such as error rates across teams of different sizes, and show progress against targets, for example 90% of target reached. The report should always show actual figures beside targets or last period, and add a sentence below each table or chart saying what it shows and what action is suggested. Too many figures confuse, so only those that support a decision should be included.
markingPoints: Tables: exact figures, with titles, headings, units and totals
Charts: suitable type for the purpose, titled and labelled with sensible scales
Averages used with care, noting unusual values
Percentages for comparison and progress against target
Shows actual versus target, adds a sentence of meaning and action, and limits figures to what is needed

essays.stem: Describe how to set up and keep an orderly filing and records system, on paper and on computer, for a team.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the types of records the team keeps, such as procedures, rotas, timesheets, reports, correspondence and customer files, and agree with the manager who may see each type. I would then set up a simple structure that is the same on paper and on the shared drive: main folders by subject, subfolders by year or month. A naming rule for electronic files, for example date, then topic, then version, such as '2026-03-14 Stock count Store 2 v2', makes files easy to find and sort. Current procedures and rotas go in a shared folder that the whole team can read, while confidential records, such as appraisals, go in restricted folders or locked cabinets. Only one master copy of each working document is kept, with version history, and old versions are moved to an archive. A retention schedule sets how long each type must be kept, based on policy and the law, and records are disposed of securely when that time ends. Electronic files are backed up. I would brief the team on the system, write it on one page, and check it each quarter.
markingPoints: Lists record types and agrees access rights
Same logical structure on paper and computer; clear naming rule
Shared folders for team documents; restricted storage for confidential records
Single master copy with version control; archive; retention schedule and secure disposal; backups
Briefs the team, documents the system and reviews it regularly

essays.stem: Explain how a supervisor should pass problems and suggestions from her team up to management.
essays.modelAnswer: A supervisor is the link between the team and management, so she must pass information upward accurately and at the right time. For a problem, she should first gather the facts: what is happening, since when, how often, what it costs or risks, and what has already been tried. She should judge urgency: safety risks, legal issues, fraud or anything that will stop work must be reported at once, directly to the right manager, and confirmed in writing. Less urgent problems can go in her regular report or meeting. She should present the problem briefly, with the facts first, then possible solutions and her recommendation, and say clearly what decision or help she needs. For suggestions from staff, she should collect them, check whether they are practical, and pass on the useful ones with the staff member's name, so credit is given. She should stay within the proper channels and not go over her manager's head unless the matter involves the manager. Finally, she must close the loop by telling the team what management decided and why, so they continue to raise issues.
markingPoints: Gathers facts: what, since when, how often, impact, what was tried
Judges urgency: safety, legal, fraud or stoppages reported at once and confirmed in writing
Presents briefly with options, a recommendation and the help needed
Passes on staff suggestions with credit, using proper channels
Closes the loop by telling the team the outcome

essays.stem: A team often makes mistakes because information does not reach everyone. Evaluate the likely causes and recommend improvements.
essays.modelAnswer: Several causes are likely. Information may be spread across too many channels, such as email, a chat group, the notice board and word of mouth, so people do not know where to look. Shift workers and part-time staff may miss briefings held when they are not on duty. Messages may be unclear, too long or full of jargon, so people misunderstand them. There may be no handover system, so information is lost between shifts. Procedures may be out of date, with old versions still in circulation. Finally, the supervisor may not check understanding, assuming that sending a message means it was received. To find the main causes, I would ask the team and trace two or three recent mistakes back to where the information failed. I would then agree which channel is used for which kind of message, introduce a short briefing at the start of every shift with a written summary for those absent, and use a standard handover log. Procedures would be kept in one shared folder with old versions removed. Key messages would be written in plain language and checked by asking staff to confirm. Error rates would be checked again after two months.
markingPoints: Identifies likely causes: too many channels, missed shifts, unclear messages
Further causes: no handover, out-of-date procedures, no check of understanding
Investigates causes with the team and by tracing mistakes
Recommends clear channel rules, shift briefings with written summaries, handover log, single source for procedures, plain language and confirmation
Measures results after the changes

practical1.title: Compile and present a weekly work activity report
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a set of raw work records for one week from a made-up team (for example the orders section of a distribution company in Spanish Town): daily output sheets, an error log, a timesheet summary and two incident notes. As a group, turn these into a two-page weekly report for the manager and give a 5-minute spoken briefing. Give each member a named role: data gatherer (collects and lists every figure with its source), data checker (re-adds totals and queries anything unusual or missing), table and chart maker (one table and one chart on screen), report writer (summary, results against targets, issues and recommended actions under clear headings), and presenter (gives the spoken briefing to the assessor acting as manager and answers questions). In a group of four, the data gatherer also checks the data, with another member checking their totals. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Raw work records from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word processor software, and a printer
photos: The list of figures with their sources
The checker's workings, with any queries marked
The table and chart on screen
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the report
Used figures that match the source records, with totals checked twice
Kept facts separate from opinions and noted any missing or unusual data
Table and chart are suitable, titled and correctly labelled
Report is organised under clear headings with the main points first
Spoken briefing gives the main point, key figures and what is needed, within the time
safety: Treat the work records as confidential; leave all copies with the assessor
Use only the made-up names given; no real staff or customer details
Lock or log off computers when away from them
Share the work fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Write a work procedure, brief the team and record feedback
practical2.brief: Choose, or take from the assessor, a routine task at the Centre or in a made-up office (for example booking a training room, handling a customer refund, or receiving a delivery). As a group, write a clear standard operating procedure (SOP) of no more than one page, make a matching notice or poster, and design a simple log form that goes with the task (for example a booking log or a handover log). Then brief another group (or the assessor) on the new procedure, check their understanding, record their feedback and revise the SOP. Give each member a named role: procedure writer, notice designer, log form designer, briefer (delivers the briefing and checks understanding with questions and a trial run), and feedback recorder (notes questions and suggested changes, and leads the revision). In a group of four, the procedure writer also leads the revision. Photograph each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Computers with word processor and printer
Flipchart paper, markers and coloured card for the notice
A sample task scenario from the assessor (if not using a Centre task)
photos: The first draft of the SOP with numbered steps
The briefing in progress, including the trial run
The feedback sheet and the revised SOP with changes marked
checklist: Took a named role and produced their part of the work
SOP has a title, purpose, numbered steps in order, and who to contact, in plain language
Notice and log form match the SOP and are clear to read
Briefing explained why the procedure matters and showed the steps
Checked understanding with open questions or a trial run, not just 'Any questions?'
Recorded feedback accurately and revised the SOP in response
safety: If using a real Centre task, do not include staff or trainee personal details
Fix posters only where the Centre allows, using safe methods (no climbing on chairs or desks)
Keep the workload fair and take short breaks
